title: When it goes wrong: repairs, plans and teaching the Italian
outcomes: Names the question each of four typical errors skipped (who guards e4, what blocks the queen before d4, what guards e5 before ...d5, where the bishop retreats after ...b6) and counts the guards before acting
Sorts an error into cheap, costly or beyond repair, and plays the engine-checked repair for the unguarded pawn on e4 and the damage-limiting moves after an early d4 or ...d5
Chooses a plan in four quiet Giuoco positions from the structure, the weak point and the worst piece, and says why the wrong plans lose material
Meets a move from outside the book with three questions (what does it threaten, what did it leave undefended, which of my plans does it change) and finds a sound reply in five deviations
Tells in unlabelled positions whether a grab, a break or a capture works, including positions where the idea does not apply
Explains the whole Italian Game to a beginner in four parts (the idea, when it works, one position, one warning) and checks the explanation against a list

steps.prompt: Write your move and one reason. Then guess how bad the position is for White.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Good players also reach worse positions: a move comes too early, a pawn is left alone, a king stays in the middle. Three questions follow. When an error has happened, how do you repair it, and can every error be repaired? From a quiet position, can you build a plan? And can you explain the whole opening to someone who has never seen it?

steps.text: **Three kinds of error.** [H] Cheap errors, like the unguarded pawn, cost less than a pawn on the engine score. Costly errors, like the early break, cost a pawn and leave only a fight. Some cannot be repaired, so the skill sits one move earlier. Before a pawn break, count the attackers and defenders of its target. [H] Counting is a first filter, not a proof: the engine can still like a break that looks one attacker short.

steps.text: **Three questions for a surprise.** When an opponent leaves the book, do not hunt for a memorised refutation. Ask: what does the move threaten, what did it leave undefended, and which of my plans does it change? Then compare the position with the nearest one you know. [H] A learner who asks these three questions meets most sidelines with a sound move, even when the move has no name.

steps.text: **Before the test.** No labels from here. 'Playable' means the engine rates the move within half a pawn of its best at depth 16: a proxy, noisy by about 0.2. 'Best move' means the engine's first choice. Count the guards before you answer, aloud if you can. Expect new positions and no hints.

steps.caption: The set-up to teach: pawns on c3 and d3, both sides castled. The bishops aim at f7 and f2; the break d4 waits until the pieces are placed.

claims.statement: One white piece, the bishop on c4, attacks f7.
One black piece, the bishop on c5, attacks f2.
The break d4 is legal here.

steps.text: **The Italian in five lines.** [I] Idea: develop fast, aim the bishops at f7 and f2, build c3 and d3, break with d4 when the pieces are placed. Works when: e4 stays guarded and the centre can stay closed while you improve. Fails when: a pawn hangs, the break comes before the pieces, or a plan ignores the weak point. Warning: count the guards first. Repair: hit the intruder.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. A beginner who knows how the pieces move has five minutes. Write (1) the idea of the Italian Game in one sentence, (2) when it works, (3) one position they could set up on a board, (4) one warning: a typical error and its cheapest repair.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Compare with a model answer. (1) Develop fast, aim at f7 and f2, break with d4 when ready. (2) It works while e4 stays guarded. (3) Set-up: pawns on c3 and d3, both sides castled. (4) Warning: an unguarded e4 costs a pawn, so play d3 before castling. Did you say when it fails? The app grades nothing; you judge. [H] Teaching exposes gaps faster than a test.

**What to remember.**
- Count the guards before you castle, break or grab.
- Errors are cheap, costly or beyond repair.
- Cheap: hit the intruder. Costly: limit the damage, then develop.
- A break usually needs the queen's file open and no fewer attackers than defenders [H].
- A plan starts from structure, weak point and worst piece.
- Surprise: what does it threaten, what is undefended, which plan changes?
- The Italian: develop, aim at f7 and f2, break when ready. It fails when a pawn hangs [I].

steps.prompt: Optional. Play one game from this Italian position as White and one as Black. You pick the level; the app marks it as a quiet record, never a gate.

steps.text: **After your games.** Did you count before you broke? Did you know your plan by move eight? When your opponent left the book, which of the three questions did you ask first? [H] Playing soon after studying tests what you understood and what you only remembered. [I] Whether the game raises understanding or only adds practice is unknown; the colour, the level and the result may tell us later.

steps.prompt: How sure are you now that you could teach the Italian Game in five minutes? Which of the four parts (idea, when it works, example, warning) is your weakest?
